<![CDATA[Hyperallergic]]>https://hyperallergic.com/https://hyperallergic.com/favicon.pngHyperallergichttps://hyperallergic.com/Ghost 6.55Mon, 03 Aug 2026 20:37:47 GMT60<![CDATA[Sharmistha Ray Transforms Pickleball Courts Into Stunning Artworks]]>https://hyperallergic.com/sharmistha-ray-transforms-pickleball-courts-into-stunning-artworks/6a60ea0d517d1b0001b88f61Mon, 03 Aug 2026 20:37:46 GMT

Pickleball aficionados in downtown Pittsburgh get to enjoy an art experience as they play thanks to artist Sharmistha Ray's vibrant floor murals.

The artist's new "Geometry of Play" installation invites the public to step into — and onto — the vibrant surfaces, pickleball paddle in hand.

Unveiled on July 16, the three courts are part of Arts Landing, a $31 million community gathering space that opened earlier this year. The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust commissioned Ray to design the courts, which will be surrounded by other public works from artists such as Thaddeus Mosley and John Peña.

"Pickleball is special in that it provides a low barrier to entry in terms of ability and cost," Ray told Hyperallergic. "It feels like a social sport, and I appreciate that about it."

Sourcing inspiration from the Indian game "Pachisi" — later adopted as "Parcheesi" in the US — Ray infuses the murals with patterns that shift and morph from different angles. A large concentric circle connects two of the courts, out of which rays of saturated color spurt and race towards the border. On the other court, a kaleidoscopic prism slices through the playing surface, as other shapes interject in an array of hues and sizes.

Best known as a co-founder of Hilma's Ghost — an experimental collective rooted in feminist and spiritual practices — Ray centers community building in much of their work. "We were never working in isolation,” Ray told Hyperallergic earlier this year. “There was always a village.”

The artist has worked with mediums like glass for other public works, such as the mosaic for Manhattan's Grand Central Station. Yet the sports paint created its own challenges, requiring Ray to color-match the available options as closely as possible to their original design. Ray designed a number of pickleball paddles with the same hues, which echo the vibrant patterns sprawling across the courts.

While they previously partook in racket sports like tennis, badminton, and squash, Ray played pickleball for the first time to better understand their project. As a proponent and creator of public art, they felt as if the mural could illuminate the democratic ethos of open recreational areas.

"Whether you come to play or simply to watch the choreography of movement unfold across the mural, I hope the work offers a moment of joy, connection, and possibility," Ray said.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Two alumni from the Interlochen Center for the Arts in Michigan have come forward with previously unreported abuse allegations against Jeffrey Epstein while he was a benefactor of the school.

The alumni's allegations against the financier, which include claims of sexual misconduct and assault, emerged during a two-year external investigation into a history of abuse at the arts boarding school and summer camp.

In addition to the new accounts about Epstein, the investigation culminated in a 97-page report in which dozens of alumni made abuse allegations against 47 adults affiliated with the school between the 1950s and the 2010s.

]]><![CDATA[Ellen Pau’s Elegy to a Vanishing Hong Kong]]>https://hyperallergic.com/ellen-paus-elegy-to-a-vanishing-hong-kong/6a70c69c5b2e060001385b63Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:56:06 GMT

Drops of water trickle down a plain white wall under a heavenly light in Ellen Pau’s 1988 video installation “She Moves 她去.” Flanked by soft white veils and a nostalgic, wooden armchair, the work introduces water as a central motif in Pau’s long-standing interest in Hong Kong as a city in constant transition, moving through cycles of lost and found.

Ellen Pau: She Moves at SculptureCenter, curated by Freya Chou and designed by technical director Rain Chan, is the first United States survey exhibition of the woman widely regarded as Hong Kong’s video art pioneer. Across 15 videos and installations spanning the late 1980s to the present, water reappears in various forms: a crying wall, swimmers diving into Victoria Harbour, the scent of tear gas. Its changing states, from melting ice to evaporating mist, become a metaphor for Hong Kong herself — “always on the verge of disappearing,” as late cultural theorist Ackbar Abbas puts it — leaving little time for reflection before new changes arrive.

The city’s rapid transformation is reflected in the afterlife of “She Moves.” Over the years, the work has been transferred across formats — NTSC to PAL, VHS to DVD — remastered, and, most recently, restored with AI. With each iteration, something is lost, and something new is layered in. That state of flux is mirrored by the installation, an intimate space that invites viewers to take a seat, temporarily occupying the position of an absent subject. Who is the “she” in the title? Could it be Pau herself, who once rested in that very chair in her home; the woman in a floral dress, who appears briefly on screen; the visitors who enter and exit the space; or even Hong Kong herself?

Upon entering the underground, labyrinthine corridor, visitors encounter a work from Pau’s ongoing, multisensory Fl0ra Zero series (2016–ongoing), “Where Have All the Flowers Gone 冇花 冇假” (2026). It starts with burnt candles attached to the wall, collected by Pau and her friends over the years from the June 4 vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. On the opposite side, strips of film negatives hang from a rack, bearing ghostly silhouettes of these candles, preserving the outline of what once was. Translated into photographic images, the candles’ shifting forms draw a parallel to the making and preservation of historical records — just as light fixes a passing moment onto film, archives preserve ephemeral experiences as material records that outlast their original time. Close to the floor lie flesh-like lumps of melted wax, remnants of “Spectre of the Will” (2019), a single-channel video installation in which an infrared camera captured visitors standing before a heated wall, translating their body temperature into live heat maps. The surrounding wax slowly melted in response to the increasing energy, recalling the blood, sweat, and lives spent in collective resistance. 

The smell of burnt bark and chemicals fills the air — intermittently released into the corridor is “Sublime,” a fragrance developed by Pau with scent specialist Xavier Tseng to recreate the smell of tear gas. Visitors may find their eyes watering as they move through the space, momentarily inhabiting the danger and vulnerability of participating in public protests. It’s a direct reference to recent protests in Hong Kong, where tear gas deployed by the police against protesters became sensory evidence of state violence and the suppression of civic expression. 

Near the end of the tunnel, a holographic flame burns atop a bloodstained-looking structure resembling the torch of the Goddess of Democracy, a symbol during the Tiananmen Square protests. As viewers approach the work, motion sensors activate, switching the video feed from crackling fire to footage of burning film strips. On one hand, the work references the traditional Chinese practice of burning offerings for the dead; on the other, it comments on the altering and erasure of public records, both elegy and critique. 

Since the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration set the terms for Hong Kong’s 1997 handover, questions around identity and autonomy have loomed over the consciousness of every local. In “She Moves,” Vera Lynn’s 1939 wartime anthem “We’ll Meet Again” plays, alluding to recent protests and migration waves in Hong Kong that split families and communities. Originally written for lovers separated by war, its promise of reunion captures the hope that, as Pau put it in her recent artist talk at the Asia Art Archives in New York, Hong Kongers will all meet again on a bright sunny day.

Ellen Pau: She Moves continues at SculptureCenter (44-19 Purves Street, Long Island City, Queens) through August 16. The exhibition was curated by Freya Chou.

]]><![CDATA[AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity]]>https://hyperallergic.com/ai-companies-are-pulping-our-humanity/6a70c2705b2e06000138599eMon, 03 Aug 2026 17:52:37 GMT

After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile. And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that.

In a sobering report by Frank Landymore in Futurism, published last Saturday, explains that Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly trained on their own slop, creating a need to train them on pre-2022 writing that is uncontaminated by AI itself — that’s the particular sales pitch made by ISBNdb, a company supplying bulk orders of books to tech companies — with purchases of between one thousand and one million volumes at a time. A “hydraulic powered cutting machine” slices off book spines and removes the pages, which are scanned and digitized before being pulped. This process of “destructive scanning” is a way to elude copyright regulations through a legal loophole, with the result being that “an AI company could be destroying some of the few remaining copies that can be found” of these books.

The destruction of books, as Servetus’s case demonstrates, is hardly a historical rarity. Nor is the pulping of books for non-ideological reasons uncommon, as publishers are responsible for destroying nearly 25% of works released each year, almost always because they didn’t sell.

Rather, what the recent revelation portends is unique and terrifying: the rapacious, cannibalistic devouring of culture so as to feed the very technology meant to replace the human. The indifference of the LLM is chilling in its own way; one imagines that if a copy of Servetus’s book fell beneath the lifeless eye of the digitizer, it would simply upload all of those theological arguments into the hungry maw of the machine, where it would only serve as fodder for the advanced plagiarism device which is artificial intelligence.

“We see a future where intelligence is a utility,” said OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, “and people buy it from us on a meter.”

This is a future where technocracy has accomplished its war against the sacred materiality and artistry of the book itself, where everything is reduced to so much predictive binary. It’s an act of literal erasure for which George Orwell’s cliched warning that “who controls the past controls the future” is restored to its original impact. LLMs swell while the shelves starve, the result being an act of libricide, of corporate indifference to the obliteration of culture, ideas, and humanity itself.

]]><![CDATA[The Thorny Politics of Protest Photography]]>https://hyperallergic.com/the-thorny-politics-of-protest-photography/6a6cc58375d29f00013c366dFri, 31 Jul 2026 20:42:45 GMT

In a 2013 essay, author Barrett Swanson asked, “At what point does the aesthetic excellence of the photograph eclipse the depicted event, or, worse, distract the viewer from inquiring into what happened?” With the synchronous explosion of digital news content and unremitting global calamity, it’s a question that strongly resonates today, particularly with photography of protest and social movements. If these images overtly flatter the protestor, they can be accused of fueling performative activism and pulling attention away from the crisis at hand; if they are too beautiful, they might conceal the real risk of violence from the state. Still, if they are too graphic, they can rob the subjects of their dignity, making a cheap spectacle of dissidence.

These are tensions of which photographer-activist Misan Harriman, who has rapidly made a name for himself documenting protests since the summer of 2020, is no doubt keenly aware.

Harriman is the subject of Andy Mundy-Castle’s new documentary Shoot the People, which follows the 48-year-old Nigerian-born Brit as he chronicles activist movements across three continents. While Harriman's evolution from an amateur photographer to the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of Vogue's September edition is impressive, more exigent is his artful representation of protests, especially (though not exclusively) those in which primarily Black and Brown people are filling the streets.

]]><![CDATA[California Exhibition to Document One of the US’s Worst Deportation Campaigns]]>https://hyperallergic.com/california-exhibition-to-document-one-of-the-uss-worst-deportation-campaigns/6a690df54232c20001c38fdbFri, 31 Jul 2026 20:38:28 GMT

Juan Garcia, history professor emeritus at the University of Arizona, grew up in South Texas in an established Mexican-American ranching family. When he was around six years old, his father abruptly abandoned his trade and relocated his nine children to Chicago.

The reasons his family left Texas were complicated, and the retired professor has since spent his career studying the political headwinds that punctuated the lives of his farmer father and his mother, who lived in the United States as an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, as they headed east.

Some of the fruits of Garcia's research and excerpts of his family story will be publicly displayed in a forthcoming exhibition at Sacramento's California Museum, entitled Help Wanted / Leave Now: "Operation Wetback" & the Revolving Door of Mass Deportation.

Organized in collaboration with historians including Garcia and labor rights activist Dolores Huerta, the bilingual exhibition revolves around "Operation Wetback," one of the US's most notorious operations to deport Mexican immigrants. ("Wetback" was a derogatory term used to refer to undocumented immigrants who may have crossed into the US through the Rio Grande.) The exhibition will open on August 13 and run through January 10, 2027.

]]><![CDATA[15 Outdoor Art Shows to See in NYC This Summer]]>https://hyperallergic.com/15-outdoor-art-shows-to-see-in-nyc-this-summer/6a6b6b5f75d29f00013a9a50Fri, 31 Jul 2026 19:40:25 GMT

You know what they say: When the heat, and smoke, and floods go away, New York comes out to play. It's finally time, and you've more than earned it. We've put together a playlist of sorts, one that takes you to islands, beaches — even bus shelters — across all five boroughs.

See the city through a different lens via giant kaleidoscopes in Pelham Bay. Have yourself a game of ping-pong on artist-designed tables at Rockaway Beach. Get a little intimate with a massive teddy bear in a courtyard in Queens. Get weird with a neural network's hallucinations in a Midtown sculpture garden. Frolic on Governors Island, my personal paradise. And if you find yourself craving a little AC, check out our list of 30 indoor exhibitions to see this summer.

It's the best time of year on the best city on earth. Live a little!

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Gabriel Orozco: Public Nature

JCDecaux Bus Shelters in New York City, Chicago, and Boston
Through Sep. 6

There’s nothing better than that moment when routine life parts like a curtain and a moment of artistic interest shines through. Like encountering one of Gabriel Orozco’s photos at a bus shelter across the city (plus Boston and Chicago). These trompe-l'oeil depictions intertwine natural and urban life — a tree shoots through a wall in one — transporting you when you least expect it.

Between Tides

Beach 67, Rockaway Beach, Beach 67th Street, Arverne, Queens
Through Sep. 13

Summer brought us to the intersection of art and athletics with basketball and soccer, but Rockaway Beach is holding down the vibe for the rest of the season with several sculptural ping-pong tables. Crafted by Moko Fukuyama, Ilana Harris-Babou, Las Hermanas Iglesias, Carlos H. Matos, Amalia Pica, and the collective SUPERFLEX, the tables function as interactive art installations that encourage play and public convening. It’s BYOP (bring your own paddle … and balls), but there are free equipment rentals available throughout the weekends!

Graciela Cassel: Nature Through Kaleidoscopes

Bartow-Pell Mansion Museum, 895 Shore Road, Pelham Bay, Bronx
Through Sep. 19

At this historic 19th-century manor house, two sculptures refract the landscape and craft it anew through steel, mirrors, and the visitor’s own gaze. Argentina-born artist Graciela Cassel offers these monumental kaleidoscopes as lenses through which we might refocus our perception of the natural world as it changes over the course of the show’s yearlong installation.

Genesis Belanger: Heads or Tails

City Hall Park, Broadway and Chambers Street, Civic Center, Manhattan
Through Nov. 15

This presentation of three sculptures by Genesis Belanger establishes City Hall Park as a rendezvous site for both reflection and recreation. Belanger calls on park visitors to embrace their own beauty, as well as that of their surroundings and broader ecosystem, with weighty sculptures that somehow manage to emphasize the lightness of life.

Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt

Museum of Modern Art, 11 West 53rd Street, Midtown, Manhattan
Through Nov. 29

Generative artificial intelligence is dependent on human output, but can it interpret our own thoughts before we externalize them? Pierre Huyghe investigates AI’s potential to realize the human imagination in an interactive, multimedia body of work in MoMA's courtyard. Born from an artificial neural network’s interpretation of recorded brain activity from a person asked to imagine a series of images, UUmwelt is also activated by visitors whose gazes alter the network’s generative imagery in real time.

Roberto Lugo: Alfarero del Barrio (Village Potter)

Madison Square Park, 11 Madison Avenue, Flatiron, Manhattan
Through Dec. 6

In this joyous display of Puerto Rican pride, Roberto Lugo adapts his singular painted ceramics into a two-part colossal sculpture series in Madison Square Park. Lugo's egalitarian urn subverts historic associations of pottery with aristocracy via portraits of his own parents alongside renowned Puerto Rican figures including Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor and Broadway composer Lin-Manuel Miranda.

Read Staff Writer Isa Farfan's report

Guardian Spirit

Brooklyn Bridge, Pier 1, and Manhattan Bridge View (Public Art Fund), Dumbo, Brooklyn
Through March 8, 2027

Three talismanic sculptures stand watch on the shores of Brooklyn, overlooking Manhattan and Governors Island. Artist Woody De Othello’s totemic guardians accompany four monumental bronzes in this installation, reimagining Kongo nkisi objects often inhabited by spirits. Together they invite us to pause and reflect on the rituals, people, and small moments of tenderness that give form to our days.

Homecoming: Chakaia Booker

Socrates Sculpture Park, 32-01 Vernon Boulevard, Long Island City, Queens
Through April 2027

Chakaia Booker, who cuts and bends tires into transfixing abstract sculptures, returns to Socrates Sculpture Park to exhibit three works she made there in the late 1990s and early 2000s. On the occasion of the park’s 40th anniversary, Homecoming reunites the sculptures with the site of their inception, whose history has been shaped by the labor of countless staff members, visitors, and artists, including Booker herself.

NYC AIDS Memorial, St. Vincent’s Triangle, Greenwich Village, Manhattan
Through May 30, 2027

Next to the historic New York City AIDS Memorial, a starlit sentinel reaches into the sky like a beacon. Artist Oscar Tuazon’s installation honors the life and work of American sculptor and performance artist Scott Burton, who died in 1989 from AIDS-related complications, by reimagining his last public commission. Though Burton's piece was decommissioned in 2022, Tuazon’s “Eternal Flame” keeps the spirit of his practice burning brightly in our collective memory.

High Line, Chelsea, Manhattan
Spring 2026–Fall 2027

Tuan Andrew Nguyen’s commission for the High Line pays homage to cultural loss and spiritual persistence through a 30-foot sandstone Buddha. The sculpture is a reference to two sixth-century statues in Afghanistan that were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001. In Nguyen’s reimagining, the statue stands tall, a symbol of resilience in the face of loss.

Read Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar's report

Public Address by Alex Strada

Various locations
Through Oct. 2027

A culmination of her multiyear artist residency with NYC’s Department of Homeless Services, Alex Strada’s Public Address transposes handwritten reflections from the residents and frontline workers of city-operated shelters onto aluminum street signs installed along the streets of four boroughs. Alongside Strada’s main installation in Columbus Park, the street-side insights of our impacted neighbors open a channel for dialogue between NYC’s “right to shelter” obligation, the increasing privatization of public space, and the worsening housing affordability crisis.

Courtyard Commission: Precious Okoyomon

MoMA PS1, 22-01 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, Queens
Through 2028

Precious Okoyomon humanizes the very institutional MoMA PS1's courtyard with a tiny forest filled with a cornucopia of plants. At the center is "The Pleasure Principle," the latest iteration of the artist's lost childhood teddy bear, which invites you to slide through its butt until you exit through its mouth. A tranquil — and welcome — patch of green in a neighborhood increasingly crowded out by tall condo buildings.

Public Art on Governors Island

Governors Island
Long-term view

Trust us, Governors Island is worth the trek, or more accurately, the short ferry ride — even more so for the wonderful public art offerings. This season, highlights are Mohawk artist Alan Michelson’s installation consisting of hundreds of thousands of oysters, drawing on New York’s little-known history as an oyster hub. Plus, Sam Van Aken’s public-orchard-as-artwork with more than 100 fruit trees, Rachel Whiteread’s ghostly cabin, Mark Dion’s mad laboratory, and more still. 

Photoville Festival

Various Locations
Long-term view

New York City’s premier photo festival stages free outdoor photography exhibitions across the five boroughs. Among the ongoing highlights are an ode to grassroots soccer communities on a global scale in Goal Click: Window to the World at the South Street Seaport, a celebration of the quiet and quotidian in My Love Letter to Queens at Astoria Park, and a closer look at a Bolivian youth subculture inspired by manga and kawaii accessories through Identity at Travers Park.

Sara Ouhaddou: Al Qalam (The Pen)

Elizabeth H. Berger Plaza, Financial District, Manhattan
Ongoing

Sara Ouhaddou’s vivid mosaics, a monument to the city’s first Arabic-speaking enclave, animate a lush plaza in Manhattan’s financial district. Ouhaddou, born in France to a Moroccan family, tenderly places her own experience as an immigrant in dialogue with the literary history of Manhattan’s “Little Syria,” a thriving neighborhood of immigrants from Syria, Lebanon, and Palestine that was dismantled by the creation of the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel in the 1940s. This work translates excerpts of works by nine of the neighborhood’s prolific writers, such as Khalil Gibran, into her own mosaic language, emulating the complex linguistic and cultural exchanges that defined the neighborhood.

Rembrandt pioneered the saleable self, but unlike his rival, Gerard Van Honthorst, he failed to reconcile his personal vision with the market.
